# OSHA 10-Hour Construction Training

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/osha-10-construction.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

OSHA 10-Hour Construction is a 10-hour OSHA Outreach Training Program course that teaches entry-level construction workers to recognize and prevent job-site hazards, including OSHA's Focus Four: falls, electrocution, struck-by, and caught-in or between. It takes at least two days (OSHA caps class time at 7.5 hours per day) and ends with an official U.S. Department of Labor OSHA 10 wallet card. Zahid Presswala teaches it on-site across Chicagoland.
What is OSHA 10-Hour Construction?

OSHA 10-Hour Construction is the most requested safety course on American job sites. It's part of OSHA's voluntary Outreach Training Program, and it gives new and entry-level workers a working knowledge of the hazards they'll face on a construction site, how to protect themselves, and what their rights are under federal law.

It is not a license or certification to perform a specific task. It is the card most general contractors, project owners, and unions in the Chicago area ask to see before a worker steps on site.

What the course covers

OSHA sets the outline for every Outreach course. The 10-hour Construction class includes:

 TopicTimeWhat you learn

 Introduction to OSHA2 hrsWorker rights, employer responsibilities, how to file a complaint, how inspections work

 Focus Four hazards4 hrsFalls, electrocution, struck-by, and caught-in or between, the leading causes of construction deaths

 Personal protective and lifesaving equipmentRequiredChoosing, wearing, and inspecting PPE

 Health hazards in constructionRequiredNoise, silica, lead, chemicals, heat, and other exposures

 Electives2+ hrsChosen for your crew, such as scaffolds, ladders and stairways, excavations, materials handling, or tools

Because Zahid chooses electives based on your work, a roofing crew spends its elective time on very different material than an electrical or concrete crew. See what's covered in OSHA 10 for the full breakdown.

Who should take OSHA 10 Construction?

 New hires and apprentices starting their first construction job.

 Laborers and tradespeople: carpenters, framers, drywall, concrete, roofing, masonry, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, painting, and demolition crews.

 Workers on projects that require a card: hospitals, universities, data centers, public works, and most large commercial jobs in Cook, DuPage, Will, Kane, and Lake counties.

 Remodelers and small contractors who want documented training for insurance and bids.

If you supervise others or are responsible for site safety, OSHA 30 Construction is the better fit. Not sure? Read OSHA 10 vs OSHA 30.

Why take it in person with Zahid?

 Taught by someone who's done the work. Zahid has 25+ years on construction and industrial sites, so the examples come from real jobs.

 At your site, on your schedule. No travel days, and the class can use your actual equipment and conditions as examples.

 In your crew's language. Classes are available in English, Gujarati, and Urdu.

 Real questions, real answers. Workers can ask about the scaffold, ladder, or trench they'll be on next week, which online courses can't offer.

 Legitimate cards. Every graduate receives an official DOL card. Here's how to verify one.

How to book an OSHA 10 Construction class

 Fill out the booking form with your headcount, location, and preferred dates.

 Zahid confirms the schedule, electives, language, and group price.

 Your crew trains on-site over two or more days and receives DOL wallet cards.

Tip: If a project start date is driving the requirement, book at least two weeks ahead. A legitimate OSHA 10 can't be finished in one day.

How long does the OSHA 10 Construction course take?
OSHA 10 is 10 contact hours. OSHA's Outreach rules limit training to 7.5 hours per day, so the class always runs at least two days. Most on-site classes are scheduled as two consecutive days.
Is the OSHA 10 card from this class official?
Yes. Zahid Presswala is an OSHA-authorized Outreach Trainer for Construction, listed in OSHA's trainer directory. Students who complete the course receive the official U.S. Department of Labor OSHA 10-Hour Construction wallet card.
When will I get my OSHA 10 card?
You leave class with proof of completion, and OSHA requires authorized trainers to issue the official wallet card within 90 days of the course. Most students receive it well before that.
Is there a test at the end of OSHA 10?
OSHA requires trainers to verify that students have learned the material. In Zahid's classes that means participation, hands-on discussion, and a short knowledge check covering the main topics.
Can you teach OSHA 10 at our job site?
Yes. On-site training is the most common format. Zahid brings everything needed and teaches at your job site trailer, shop, office, or a nearby venue anywhere in Chicagoland.
How much does OSHA 10 Construction cost?
On-site group classes are quoted per group, so the per-person cost goes down as your headcount goes up. Send your headcount and location through the booking form for a quote. See our OSHA 10 and 30 cost guide for typical market prices.

# OSHA 30-Hour Construction Training

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/osha-30-construction.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

OSHA 30-Hour Construction is a 30-hour OSHA Outreach Training Program course for foremen, supervisors, and anyone with safety responsibility on a construction site. It covers hazard recognition in depth, plus how to manage safety on a crew, and takes at least four days (OSHA caps class time at 7.5 hours per day). Graduates receive an official U.S. Department of Labor OSHA 30 wallet card. Zahid Presswala teaches it on-site across Chicagoland.
What is OSHA 30-Hour Construction?

OSHA 30-Hour Construction is the supervisor-level course in OSHA's Outreach Training Program. Where OSHA 10 teaches a worker to protect themselves, OSHA 30 teaches a leader to protect a crew: spotting hazards before work starts, planning around them, and building the habits that keep a site out of trouble with OSHA.

What the course covers

OSHA 30 Construction includes all the core topics from OSHA 10, in more depth, plus a wider range of construction hazards and safety management topics:

 Introduction to OSHA, worker rights, employer duties, and how inspections and citations work

 Managing safety and health: programs, inspections, accident investigation, and working with subcontractors

 The Focus Four in depth: falls, electrocution, struck-by, and caught-in or between

 Personal protective and lifesaving equipment and health hazards such as silica, noise, lead, and heat

 Stairways and ladders, scaffolds, excavations and trenching

 Cranes, derricks, hoists, and rigging

 Concrete and masonry, steel erection, materials handling, and tools

 Electives chosen for your work, such as confined spaces, fire protection, motor vehicles, or welding and cutting

Who should take OSHA 30 Construction?

 Foremen, lead hands, and crew chiefs

 Superintendents and assistant superintendents

 Project managers and owners of small contracting companies

 Safety coordinators and anyone designated to run a site safety program

 Experienced workers stepping up to a lead role

A common pattern for Chicago-area contractors: the whole crew takes OSHA 10, and every lead takes OSHA 30.

Scheduling OSHA 30 around your projects

The hardest part of OSHA 30 is usually pulling supervisors off the job for four days. On-site training solves that with flexible scheduling:

 Four or five consecutive days during a slow week

 One day a week for four to five weeks

 Shared sessions with supervisors from partner companies to split cost

Whichever schedule you choose, OSHA requires the course to be completed within six months, and Zahid will plan the dates with you up front.

How to book

 Send the booking form with headcount, location, and preferred schedule.

 Zahid confirms dates, electives, and group pricing.

 Supervisors complete the course and receive official DOL 30-hour cards.

How long does OSHA 30 Construction take?
OSHA 30 is 30 contact hours. With OSHA's 7.5-hour daily limit, it takes at least four days. On-site classes can run four or five consecutive days or be spread over several weeks so supervisors aren't pulled off the job all at once.
Do I need OSHA 10 before OSHA 30?
No. OSHA 30 is a standalone course. Supervisors can go straight into OSHA 30 without taking OSHA 10 first.
Who needs an OSHA 30 card?
OSHA 30 is designed for foremen, supervisors, superintendents, and safety staff. Many Chicago-area general contractors and project owners require at least one OSHA 30 holder on site, and some states, such as Nevada, require it for construction supervisors by law.
Does an OSHA 30 card make me a competent person?
Not by itself. OSHA defines a competent person by their knowledge and their authority to correct hazards on a specific site. OSHA 30 builds a strong foundation, but employers must still designate competent persons and provide task-specific training for things like scaffolds and excavations.
Can supervisors from several companies train together?
Yes. Group sessions at a shared venue are a good way for smaller contractors to split the cost of an OSHA 30 class.

# OSHA 10-Hour General Industry Training

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/osha-10-general-industry.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

OSHA 10-Hour General Industry is a 10-hour OSHA Outreach Training Program course for entry-level workers in warehouses, manufacturing plants, healthcare, retail, and other non-construction workplaces. It follows 29 CFR 1910 and covers walking-working surfaces, emergency action plans, electrical safety, PPE, and hazard communication. It takes at least two days and ends with an official DOL OSHA 10 wallet card. Zahid Presswala teaches it on-site across Chicagoland.
What is OSHA 10-Hour General Industry?

OSHA 10-Hour General Industry is the entry-level Outreach course for every workplace that isn't a construction site: distribution centers, manufacturing plants, machine shops, food processing, hospitals and clinics, hotels, retail stores, and building maintenance. It teaches workers to recognize the hazards most often behind injuries and OSHA citations in those settings.

What the course covers

The required core topics are set by OSHA:

 Introduction to OSHA: worker rights, employer responsibilities, and how to report hazards

 Walking and working surfaces: slips, trips, falls, ladders, and dock edges

 Exit routes, emergency action plans, and fire prevention

 Electrical safety

 Personal protective equipment

 Hazard communication: labels, safety data sheets, and chemical safety

Elective time is matched to your operation. Common choices include powered industrial trucks (forklifts), machine guarding, lockout/tagout, materials handling, ergonomics, and bloodborne pathogens.

Who should take it?

 Warehouse and distribution workers along the I-55, I-80, I-88, and I-90 corridors

 Production, assembly, and machine operators

 Maintenance technicians and facility staff

 Healthcare support, environmental services, and food service teams

 New hires at any company that wants documented baseline safety training

Supervisors and safety coordinators should consider OSHA 30 General Industry. Not sure if you're construction or general industry? See this guide.

Why on-site training works better for facilities

 Your hazards, not generic ones. Zahid uses your docks, racking, machines, and chemicals as examples.

 Shift-friendly. Sessions can be scheduled for any shift without sending people offsite.

 Language access. English, Gujarati, and Urdu instruction for multilingual workforces.

 One record for the whole team. Everyone trains together and is documented together.

How to book

 Fill out the booking form with your headcount, shifts, and location.

 Zahid confirms the schedule, electives, and group price.

 Your team trains on-site and every graduate receives a DOL wallet card.

What is the difference between OSHA 10 General Industry and OSHA 10 Construction?
General Industry follows 29 CFR 1910 and is for fixed workplaces like warehouses, plants, hospitals, and stores. Construction follows 29 CFR 1926 and is for building, renovation, and demolition work. Pick the one that matches where you work most.
Can you schedule OSHA 10 around our shifts?
Yes. Classes can run across two full days or be split into shorter sessions that fit first, second, or third shift, as long as no day exceeds OSHA's 7.5-hour limit.
Does OSHA 10 General Industry cover forklifts?
Powered industrial trucks can be included as an elective. Note that OSHA 10 does not replace the separate forklift operator training and evaluation OSHA requires under 1910.178.
How many workers can attend one class?
OSHA limits Outreach classes to 40 students per trainer. For larger workforces, Zahid can run several sessions back to back.

# OSHA 30-Hour General Industry Training

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/osha-30-general-industry.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

OSHA 30-Hour General Industry is a 30-hour OSHA Outreach Training Program course for supervisors, managers, and safety coordinators in warehouses, manufacturing, healthcare, and other non-construction workplaces. It follows 29 CFR 1910 and covers safety program management plus hazards like lockout/tagout, machine guarding, forklifts, and confined spaces. It takes at least four days and ends with an official DOL OSHA 30 wallet card. Zahid Presswala teaches it on-site across Chicagoland.
What is OSHA 30-Hour General Industry?

OSHA 30 General Industry is the most complete course in OSHA's Outreach Training Program for non-construction workplaces. It goes beyond hazard recognition and teaches supervisors how to run safety: inspecting, correcting, documenting, and leading a team that works safely when no one is watching.

What the course covers

 Introduction to OSHA and managing safety and health programs

 Walking-working surfaces and fall protection

 Exit routes, emergency action plans, fire prevention, and fire protection

 Electrical safety and personal protective equipment

 Hazard communication and industrial hygiene basics

 Lockout/tagout (control of hazardous energy)

 Machine guarding and powered industrial trucks

 Permit-required confined spaces

 Ergonomics, bloodborne pathogens, welding and cutting, and recordkeeping, depending on electives

Several of these, including lockout/tagout, machine guarding, forklifts, and hazard communication, appear on OSHA's most-cited standards list every year. That's why supervisors who understand them save their companies money.

Who should take it?

 Production, warehouse, and shift supervisors

 Plant, operations, and facility managers

 EHS and safety coordinators, especially those new to the role

 Maintenance managers and lead technicians

 Owners of small manufacturing, logistics, or service businesses

What employers get out of it

 Supervisors who can spot and fix the hazards behind the most common citations

 Better incident investigation and recordkeeping

 A stronger case when customers, insurers, or auditors ask about training

 Lower risk of costly OSHA penalties. See current penalty amounts

How to book

 Send the booking form with your headcount, location, and schedule.

 Zahid confirms dates, electives, and pricing.

 Supervisors complete the course on-site and receive official DOL 30-hour cards.

Who should take OSHA 30 General Industry?
Anyone who supervises workers or is responsible for safety in a general industry workplace: shift supervisors, production and warehouse managers, maintenance leads, EHS coordinators, and owners of small facilities.
How long does OSHA 30 General Industry take?
At least four days, because OSHA limits Outreach training to 7.5 hours per day. On-site classes can run on consecutive days or be spread over several weeks.
Does OSHA 30 cover OSHA recordkeeping?
Yes. Supervisors learn the basics of OSHA injury and illness recordkeeping, including the OSHA 300 log, along with how to run inspections and investigate incidents.
Is OSHA 30 General Industry harder than OSHA 10?
It covers more topics in more depth and focuses on managing safety, not just personal protection. Zahid keeps it practical with examples from your own facility.

OSHA training in Chicago

Chicago is one of the busiest construction and industrial markets in the country, and most serious projects here expect workers to show up with an OSHA card. From high-rise and mixed-use work downtown to hospital, university, transit, and airport projects, general contractors and owners routinely require OSHA 10 for every worker and OSHA 30 for supervisors. Zahid brings the full course to your Chicago job site, shop, or office so your crew doesn't lose days traveling to a classroom.

Who we train in Chicago

 High-rise, mixed-use, and tenant build-out crews in the Loop, River North, West Loop, and Fulton Market

 Hospital, university, and institutional construction and facilities teams

 Infrastructure, transit, and airport contractors around O'Hare and Midway

 Manufacturers, food processors, and distribution centers on the South and West Sides

 Property management and building maintenance teams across the city

Courses available in Chicago

 CourseBest forLength

 OSHA 10 ConstructionConstruction workers and new hires10 hrs, 2+ days

 OSHA 30 ConstructionForemen, supervisors, safety leads30 hrs, 4+ days

 OSHA 10 General IndustryWarehouse, plant, and facility staff10 hrs, 2+ days

 OSHA 30 General IndustrySupervisors and safety coordinators30 hrs, 4+ days

What Chicago employers should know

Private employers in Chicago are covered by federal OSHA, while City of Chicago and other public employees are covered by Illinois OSHA. Illinois has no blanket state law requiring OSHA 10 cards, but in Chicago the requirement almost always arrives through the contract: owners, general contractors, unions, and public agencies write OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 into bid documents and site rules. If you are bidding on larger Chicago work, get your crew carded before mobilization.

Plan ahead: a legitimate OSHA 10 takes at least two days and OSHA 30 at least four, because OSHA limits Outreach training to 7.5 hours per day. Any "one-day OSHA 10" offer is a red flag. See how to spot a fake card.

Most larger Chicago projects do. The requirement usually comes from the owner, general contractor, union, or public agency rather than a city ordinance, and OSHA 30 is commonly required for foremen and supervisors.

# OSHA 10 & 30 Training in Bolingbrook, IL

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/locations/osha-training-bolingbrook.html

# OSHA 10 & 30 Training in Gujarati

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/osha-training-gujarati.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

Yes, you can take official OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 training in Gujarati. Zahid Presswala, an OSHA-authorized Outreach Trainer for Construction and General Industry, teaches the full courses in Gujarati (as well as English and Urdu) on-site at your workplace in Chicagoland, and nationwide by arrangement. Graduates receive the same official U.S. Department of Labor OSHA wallet card as any English-language class.
Why learn OSHA safety in Gujarati?

Safety training only works if it's understood. Workers who learn in their first language catch details that get lost in translation: what a guardrail height really means, why a ladder angle matters, what a chemical label is warning about. They also ask more questions, which is where real learning happens.

OSHA itself requires that training be presented in a language and vocabulary workers understand. A Gujarati-language class is one of the clearest ways to meet that expectation for Gujarati-speaking crews.

Courses available in Gujarati

 OSHA 10-Hour Construction for workers on building, renovation, and remodeling sites

 OSHA 30-Hour Construction for foremen, supervisors, and contractors

 OSHA 10-Hour General Industry for hotels, warehouses, stores, and plants

 OSHA 30-Hour General Industry for managers and owners

Who books Gujarati OSHA classes?

 Hotel and motel owners and staff who need General Industry training for maintenance and housekeeping teams

 Construction and remodeling contractors whose crews and subcontractors speak Gujarati

 Gas station, convenience store, and retail owners who want documented safety training

 Trucking, warehouse, and logistics companies

 Manufacturers and shops with multilingual workforces

How to book a Gujarati-language class

 Fill out the booking form and mention that you want the class in Gujarati.

 Zahid will call you, in Gujarati if you prefer, to confirm the course, schedule, and price.

 Your team trains on-site and every graduate receives an official DOL wallet card.

Prefer to talk first? Call (847) 863-4798.

Is an OSHA card from a Gujarati-language class official?
Yes. OSHA allows authorized trainers to teach Outreach courses in languages other than English when the trainer is fluent. The card is the same U.S. Department of Labor wallet card, and it is printed in English.
Can my crew mix Gujarati and English speakers in one class?
Yes. Zahid can teach in English and explain key points in Gujarati (or Urdu) so everyone in a mixed group follows along.
Do you teach Gujarati OSHA classes outside Illinois?
Yes, by arrangement. Many Gujarati-owned businesses, including hotels, construction companies, and logistics firms, are spread across the country. Contact Zahid with your location and group size.
Are the course materials in Gujarati?
Instruction, discussion, and explanations are in Gujarati. Some written materials and the OSHA standards themselves are in English, and Zahid explains them in Gujarati as the class goes.
શું ગુજરાતીમાં OSHA 10 કરી શકાય? (Can I take OSHA 10 in Gujarati?)
Yes. Zahid teaches OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 fully in Gujarati. Call (847) 863-4798 or use the booking form.

Classes are held on-site in Chicagoland or nationwide by arrangement, and graduates receive the official U.S. Department of Labor OSHA wallet card.
Why take OSHA training in Urdu?

Many workers can get by in English on the job, but safety training is where "getting by" isn't enough. Learning in Urdu means workers understand why a rule exists, not just what it says, and they're far more likely to speak up when something looks wrong.

OSHA expects employers to present training in a language workers understand. An Urdu-language Outreach course meets that expectation and gives every worker the same official card.

Can I take OSHA 10 in Hindi?
Zahid teaches in Urdu, which shares everyday spoken vocabulary and grammar with Hindi. Most Hindi speakers follow an Urdu-language class easily. Technical terms are explained in plain language, with the English OSHA term alongside.

Yes. It is the same official U.S. Department of Labor Outreach wallet card. The card itself is printed in English.

# On-Site OSHA Training for Employers

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/on-site-osha-training.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

On-site OSHA training means an OSHA-authorized Outreach Trainer comes to your job site, shop, or office and teaches OSHA 10 or OSHA 30 to your group in person. Zahid Presswala offers on-site Construction and General Industry classes throughout Chicagoland, with group pricing, flexible scheduling, instruction in English, Gujarati, or Urdu, and an official DOL wallet card for every graduate.
How on-site OSHA training works

 Tell us what you need. Use the booking form to share your industry, headcount, location, language, and dates.

 Get a quote and a plan. Zahid confirms the right course, picks electives that match your hazards, and sets a schedule that fits your shifts.

 Train on-site. Your team completes the course where they work, with examples drawn from your equipment and conditions.

 Get carded. Each graduate gets proof of completion, and official DOL wallet cards follow (OSHA requires them within 90 days).

Why employers choose on-site training

 On-site with ZahidSending workers outOnline course

 Travel timeNoneCommutes, mileageNone

 Tailored to your hazardsYesSometimesNo

 Live Q&A with a trainerYesYesLimited

 Language optionsEnglish, Gujarati, UrduVariesUsually English or Spanish

 Everyone done at onceYesStaggeredHard to track

 Group pricingYesRarelySometimes

For a deeper comparison, read online vs in-person OSHA training.

Industries we train on-site

 Construction: general contractors, concrete, framing, drywall, roofing, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, excavation, and remodeling.

 Warehousing and logistics: distribution centers, cold storage, freight, and fulfillment.

 Manufacturing: metal fabrication, food processing, plastics, printing, and assembly.

 Facilities and property management: maintenance teams for commercial, residential, healthcare, and education buildings.

 Hospitality, retail, and healthcare support teams that need General Industry training.

Where we train

Zahid is based in Naperville and trains on-site across Chicagoland, including Chicago, Naperville, Aurora, Joliet, Bolingbrook, Schaumburg, Elgin, Downers Grove, Oak Brook, Elk Grove Village, and Wheaton. See all service areas.

What do we need to provide for an on-site class?
A room or trailer that seats your group, tables or chairs, and a wall or screen for slides. Zahid brings the course materials. Access to your actual work area for examples is helpful but not required.
What is the minimum group size?
There's no strict minimum. On-site classes are most cost-effective for groups of about five or more. Smaller groups can join a shared session.
Can several companies share one class?
Yes. General contractors often bring their subcontractors together, and small companies split a session to share costs.
How far will you travel?
Zahid is based in Naperville and regularly teaches throughout Chicago and the suburbs in Cook, DuPage, Will, Kane, Lake, and McHenry counties. Travel elsewhere in Illinois and other states is available by arrangement.
Can you train on weekends or night shift?
Often, yes. Include your preferred days and times in the booking form.

# OSHA 10 vs OSHA 30: Which Card Do You Actually Need?

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/osha-10-vs-osha-30.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

OSHA 10 is a 10-hour course for entry-level workers that teaches basic hazard recognition and worker rights. OSHA 30 is a 30-hour course for supervisors, foremen, and anyone with safety responsibility, covering the same foundations in far more depth plus how to manage safety on a site. If you direct other people's work, take OSHA 30. If you're new to the trade, start with OSHA 10.
The short version

I get this question more than any other, usually from someone who's just been told by a foreman or a GC that they "need their OSHA card." The answer depends on one thing: are you responsible for other people's safety on the job?

 If you're a laborer, apprentice, new hire, warehouse associate, or tradesperson doing the work yourself, OSHA 10 is the standard.

 If you're a foreman, superintendent, crew lead, safety coordinator, project manager, or business owner, OSHA 30 is the right fit.

OSHA 10 vs OSHA 30 side by side

 OSHA 10OSHA 30

 Designed forEntry-level workersSupervisors and workers with safety responsibility

 Length10 contact hours30 contact hours

 Minimum days2 (7.5-hour daily cap)4 (7.5-hour daily cap)

 FocusRecognizing and avoiding common hazards, worker rightsSame foundation in more depth, plus more standards and managing safety

 PrerequisiteNoneNone (OSHA 10 not required first)

 CardDOL 10-Hour wallet cardDOL 30-Hour wallet card

 VersionsConstruction, General Industry, MaritimeConstruction, General Industry, Maritime

What OSHA 10 covers

OSHA 10 is built to give a worker the vocabulary and awareness to spot hazards and speak up. In the Construction version, most of the required time goes to:

 Introduction to OSHA: your rights, employer responsibilities, how to file a complaint, and how inspections work.

 The Focus Four hazards: falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution, which together cause most construction deaths. (Read more in our Focus Four guide.)

 PPE and health hazards: hard hats, eye and hearing protection, silica, noise, and chemicals.

 Electives: topics like scaffolds, ladders, stairways, materials handling, and excavation, chosen by the trainer to fit the group.

The General Industry version follows the same idea with topics like walking-working surfaces, emergency action plans, electrical safety, and hazard communication.

What OSHA 30 adds

OSHA 30 is not just "OSHA 10, three times longer." The extra 20 hours go into topics a supervisor needs to plan and run safe work:

 Deeper coverage of fall protection, excavations and trenching, scaffolding, and electrical systems.

 Cranes, rigging, concrete and masonry, and steel erection (Construction), or lockout/tagout, confined spaces, and powered industrial trucks (General Industry).

 Safety and health programs, hazard prevention planning, and managing subcontractors.

 Recordkeeping basics and what happens during and after an OSHA inspection.

From the field: The supervisors who get the most out of OSHA 30 are the ones who bring real problems from their own site. Bring your questions about that one ladder setup or trench that always worries you. That's what the class is for.

Who requires which card?

Federal OSHA does not require workers to hold an Outreach card. But plenty of others do:

 States: Several states, including New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island, require OSHA 10 for certain construction work, especially public projects. Some require OSHA 30 for supervisors.

 Cities: New York City, for example, has its own Site Safety Training requirements that build on OSHA courses.

 Contractors and owners: Many general contractors, school districts, hospitals, and large facilities require OSHA 10 for everyone on site and OSHA 30 for supervisors.

 Unions and employers: Many build Outreach training into apprenticeships and onboarding.

If you're in Illinois, see our guide to OSHA training in Illinois.

How much do OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 cost?

Pricing varies by format. Self-paced online courses from OSHA-accepted providers commonly run under $100 for OSHA 10 and roughly $150 to $200 for OSHA 30. In-person classes are often priced per group, which can make on-site training cost-effective for a crew, especially once you count the value of hands-on discussion and a trainer who can answer questions about your actual site. Request a group quote for on-site pricing.

How to choose for your crew

For employers, the most common setup I see works well:

 Put every field worker through OSHA 10 in the version that matches your work.

 Put foremen, leads, and anyone who signs off on work through OSHA 30.

 Back it up with regular toolbox talks and task-specific training, since OSHA standards require training on specific hazards (like fall protection or forklifts) that an Outreach course alone does not satisfy.

Is OSHA 30 better than OSHA 10?
Not better, just deeper. OSHA 30 covers more topics in more detail and is aimed at people with safety responsibility. For an entry-level worker, OSHA 10 is usually what an employer or job site asks for.
Do I need OSHA 10 before I can take OSHA 30?
No. OSHA 30 is a standalone course. You can go straight into OSHA 30, and it satisfies any requirement for a 10-hour card in the same industry.
Does an OSHA 30 card count if a job requires OSHA 10?
In almost every case, yes. OSHA 30 includes everything in OSHA 10 for the same industry. Check the specific requirement if it's a state law or contract, but a 30-hour card is generally accepted wherever a 10-hour card is required.
How long is each course?
OSHA 10 is 10 contact hours and OSHA 30 is 30 contact hours. Because OSHA limits Outreach training to 7.5 hours per day, OSHA 10 takes at least two days and OSHA 30 takes at least four.
Is OSHA 10 or OSHA 30 a certification?
Technically, neither is a certification. OSHA calls the card proof of completing Outreach training. It shows you took the course; it does not certify you to operate equipment or perform specific tasks.


---

# How to Get Your OSHA 10 Card: Step-by-Step Guide

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/how-to-get-osha-10-card.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

To get an OSHA 10 card: (1) choose Construction or General Industry, (2) enroll with an OSHA-authorized Outreach trainer or an OSHA-accepted online provider, (3) complete all 10 contact hours over at least two days and pass the course assessment, and (4) receive your official Department of Labor wallet card, which trainers must issue within 90 days.
Step 1: Choose the right industry

OSHA 10 comes in two main versions, and the card says which one you took:

 Construction if you build, renovate, demolish, paint, roof, or do electrical, plumbing, or HVAC work on construction projects.

 General Industry if you work in a warehouse, plant, distribution center, healthcare facility, retail, or most other fixed workplaces.

A Construction card won't satisfy a General Industry requirement and vice versa. If you're not sure, our Construction vs General Industry guide breaks it down.

Step 2: Find a legitimate trainer or provider

A real OSHA 10 card is a U.S. Department of Labor card issued through the OSHA Outreach Training Program. You can earn one in two ways:

 In person with an OSHA-authorized Outreach trainer. You can look up any trainer in OSHA's trainer directory. (Here's Zahid's listing.)

 Online with one of a small number of OSHA-accepted online Outreach providers listed on OSHA's website.

Red flags: "Get your OSHA card today," prices that seem too good to be true, no identity checks, or a provider that can't name the authorized trainer behind the course. Fake cards are a real problem, and an employer or inspector can reject them.

Step 3: Complete all 10 hours

OSHA sets rules that every legitimate course follows:

 10 contact hours of instruction, covering required topics plus electives.

 No more than 7.5 hours per day, so the course spans at least two days.

 Online courses must be completed within six months of starting, and include knowledge checks and a final exam.

 In-person classes require you to attend the whole course. Missing part of it means you don't get a card until you make it up.

In an on-site class, we usually schedule two consecutive days at your job site or shop. Your crew learns together, asks questions about their actual work, and nobody has to fight with a slow website.

Step 4: Receive your DOL wallet card

When you finish, you'll typically get a completion certificate right away. The official plastic DOL card comes from the trainer or provider, and OSHA requires it to be issued within 90 days. Modern cards include security features that make them harder to fake.

When it arrives, check that your name is spelled correctly and the industry (Construction or General Industry) and course (10-hour) are right.

How long does the whole process take?

 StageTypical time

 Booking an on-site classAbout a week, depending on availability

 The course itself2 days minimum

 Completion certificateSame day as completion

 Official DOL cardUp to 90 days (often sooner)

How much does an OSHA 10 card cost?

Online OSHA 10 courses from accepted providers commonly cost under $100 per person. In-person classes vary by trainer, location, and group size. For employers training several workers, on-site group pricing is often competitive with per-seat online pricing and avoids lost time from workers clicking through modules on their own. Get a quote for your crew.

After you get your card

An OSHA 10 card is a starting point, not the finish line. It shows you've had basic hazard awareness training. Your employer is still responsible for training you on the specific hazards and equipment you work with. If your job needs more than OSHA 10, read OSHA 10 vs OSHA 30, and check whether your card ever needs renewing in Do OSHA cards expire?

Can I get my OSHA 10 card in one day?
No. OSHA limits Outreach training to a maximum of 7.5 hours per day, so a legitimate OSHA 10 course always spans at least two days. Anyone offering a same-day OSHA 10 card is not following OSHA rules.
How long does it take to receive the physical card?
OSHA requires authorized trainers to provide cards to students within 90 days of course completion. Many students receive theirs sooner, and most providers give a completion certificate you can show an employer in the meantime.
Is there a test for OSHA 10?
Yes. Outreach courses include knowledge checks and a final assessment. Online courses require a passing score on the final exam, and trainers verify that students participated in the full course.
What if I lose my OSHA 10 card?
Contact the trainer or online provider who issued it. Replacement cards are limited and are generally only available for a set number of years after training, so contact them as soon as you notice it's missing.
Can I get an OSHA 10 card in Spanish or another language?
Yes. Outreach courses can be taught in other languages by trainers who are fluent in them. Zahid teaches in English, Gujarati, and Urdu.


---

# Do OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 Cards Expire?

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/do-osha-cards-expire.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

No. OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 cards issued through the federal Outreach Training Program do not expire. However, some states (such as Nevada), cities (such as New York City), employers, unions, and project owners require workers to retake the course or complete refresher training, commonly every 3 to 5 years.
The federal rule: no expiration

OSHA's Outreach Training Program is voluntary, and the cards it produces are proof that you completed a course. They're not licenses, so federal OSHA puts no expiration date on them. A card earned in 2012 is still a valid record that you took the course in 2012.

That said, the date on the card matters more than most people think.

When OSHA cards effectively "expire"

State and local laws

Some places that require Outreach training also require it to be renewed:

 Nevada requires OSHA 10 for construction workers and OSHA 30 for supervisors, and requires renewal every five years.

 New York City requires Site Safety Training (SST) cards for many construction workers. OSHA courses count toward the hours, and SST cards must be renewed every five years.

 Other states, such as New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Missouri, require OSHA 10 for certain public construction work. Some also require supervisors to hold OSHA 30. Rules differ, and some set their own timeframes.

Employer and project requirements

This is where most workers run into it. General contractors, facility owners, hospitals, universities, and unions often write their own rules into contracts and site policies, such as "OSHA 10 within the last five years" or "OSHA 30 for all supervisors, renewed every three years." These rules are just as binding on that job as a law would be.

Lost cards

If you lose an old card, you may not be able to replace it. Trainers and providers can only issue replacements for a limited period after the class. After that, the only way to prove your training is to take it again.

Should you retake OSHA 10 or 30 even if you don't have to?

From years of teaching, my honest answer is yes, if it's been more than about five years. Here's why:

 Standards change. Respirable silica, hazard communication updates, walking-working surface rules, and penalty amounts have all changed in the last decade.

 Your role changes. If you've moved up to lead or foreman since your OSHA 10, it's time for OSHA 30.

 Habits drift. A refresher is a chance to reset the shortcuts that creep in on every crew.

How to keep your crew's cards current

 Keep a simple spreadsheet with each worker's card type, industry, and completion date.

 Flag anyone approaching 5 years, or whatever period your projects require.

 Schedule one on-site class for everyone due, instead of sending people out one at a time.

Need to refresh a group? Book an on-site class and Zahid will train everyone at once.

How long is an OSHA 10 card good for?
Under federal rules, indefinitely. The card shows you completed the training and doesn't carry an expiration date. Check your state, city, employer, or project requirements, since some only accept cards from the last 3 to 5 years.
Does Nevada require OSHA 10 renewal?
Yes. Nevada requires construction workers to complete OSHA 10 and supervisors to complete OSHA 30, and requires the training to be renewed every five years.
Do I have to retake the whole course to renew?
Usually, yes. There is no official federal 'OSHA 10 refresher' card. When a state, employer, or project requires renewal, workers generally retake the full 10 or 30-hour course and receive a new card with a new completion date.
What if I lost my old card?
Contact the trainer or provider who issued it. Replacements are limited and generally only available for a set period after the course. If that window has passed, you'll need to take the course again.


---

# OSHA Construction vs General Industry: Which Course Is Right for You?

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/construction-vs-general-industry.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

Take the Construction course if your work involves building, altering, repairing, painting, or demolishing structures (OSHA 29 CFR 1926). Take General Industry if you work in a fixed workplace like a warehouse, factory, hospital, store, or office (29 CFR 1910). Maintenance work generally falls under General Industry, while construction, alteration, and major repair work falls under Construction.
Two sets of OSHA rules

OSHA standards are split by industry. The two you'll hear about most:

 29 CFR 1926 (Construction): rules for construction, alteration, repair, painting, decorating, and demolition work.

 29 CFR 1910 (General Industry): rules for most other workplaces, including manufacturing, warehousing, healthcare, retail, and services.

Outreach courses are built around these standards, which is why OSHA 10 and 30 come in separate Construction and General Industry versions.

Quick decision guide

 Your jobUsually take

 Carpenter, laborer, roofer, ironworker, masonConstruction

 Electrician, plumber, HVAC on construction projectsConstruction

 Painter or drywall installer on job sitesConstruction

 Excavation, paving, or demolition crewConstruction

 Warehouse or distribution center workerGeneral Industry

 Manufacturing or production workerGeneral Industry

 Facility or building maintenance technicianGeneral Industry

 Hospital, hotel, or retail staffGeneral Industry

 Forklift operator in a plantGeneral Industry

 Foreman or superintendent on construction sitesConstruction (OSHA 30)

 Plant safety coordinator or supervisorGeneral Industry (OSHA 30)

What each course focuses on

Construction

 The Focus Four: falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, electrocution

 Scaffolds, ladders, and stairways

 Excavation and trenching

 Cranes, rigging, and heavy equipment (more in OSHA 30)

 Health hazards like silica, noise, and lead

General Industry

 Walking-working surfaces and fall protection

 Emergency action plans, fire prevention, and exit routes

 Electrical safety

 Hazard communication and chemical safety

 Machine guarding, lockout/tagout, and powered industrial trucks (forklifts)

The maintenance gray area

This trips up a lot of facility teams. OSHA generally looks at the nature of the work:

 Maintenance: keeping a building or equipment in its existing condition, such as replacing a motor with the same model or patching a roof. This is generally General Industry.

 Construction: building, altering, or significantly upgrading, such as adding a mezzanine, re-wiring a production line, or remodeling an office. This is generally Construction.

If your maintenance staff regularly do both, it often makes sense to train them in General Industry and give the leads Construction OSHA 30, or vice versa. I'm happy to help you think it through when you request training.

Before you book: ask these three questions

 What does the requirement say? If a contract, site policy, or state law requires a card, it will usually specify the industry.

 Where does most of your work happen? A construction project or a fixed facility?

 What's your role? Workers take OSHA 10; supervisors take OSHA 30. See OSHA 10 vs OSHA 30.

Can I use a General Industry OSHA 10 card on a construction site?
Usually not. Construction sites and contracts that require OSHA 10 almost always mean the Construction version. Check the specific requirement, but plan on Construction for construction work.
Is maintenance construction or general industry?
OSHA generally treats routine maintenance (keeping equipment and facilities in their existing condition) as general industry, and construction, alteration, or major repair work as construction. The line can be blurry, so for mixed roles talk to a trainer about your actual tasks.
Which course is harder?
Neither is harder. They cover different standards. Construction spends more time on falls, scaffolds, trenching, and the Focus Four. General Industry spends more time on machine guarding, lockout/tagout, forklifts, and hazard communication.
I'm an electrician. Which do I take?
If you mostly work on construction projects (new builds, renovations), take Construction. If you're an in-house electrician maintaining a plant or building, General Industry is usually the better fit.

# The OSHA Focus Four Hazards in Construction, Explained

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/focus-four-hazards.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

The OSHA Focus Four hazards are falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution. Together they cause the majority of construction worker deaths in the United States, with falls the leading cause. They're sometimes called the "Fatal Four," and they make up a required part of every OSHA 10 and 30-Hour Construction course.
Why OSHA focuses on these four

Year after year, falls, struck-by incidents, caught-in or between incidents, and electrocutions account for most construction worker deaths in the U.S. If a crew truly understands these four hazards, it eliminates most of the ways people get killed on a job site. That's why the Construction OSHA 10 spends a large share of its required hours here.

1. Falls

Falls are the number one killer in construction. They happen from roofs, ladders, scaffolds, unprotected edges, and through holes and skylights.

How to prevent falls

 Use guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall arrest systems at 6 feet or more in construction.

 Cover and label floor holes and skylights, and secure covers so they can't shift.

 Set ladders on stable footing, extend them 3 feet above the landing, and maintain three points of contact.

 Have scaffolds erected and inspected by a competent person.

 Inspect harnesses and lanyards before every use.

Go deeper in our OSHA fall protection guide.

2. Struck-by

Struck-by incidents happen when a worker is hit by a moving object: a vehicle or piece of equipment, a falling tool or material, or a flying object from a tool or a failed part.

How to prevent struck-by injuries

 Wear high-visibility clothing around vehicles and equipment.

 Never stand behind backing equipment or between equipment and a fixed object; use spotters.

 Use toe boards, debris nets, and tool lanyards when working overhead.

 Stay out from under suspended loads.

 Wear hard hats, and eye and face protection for tasks that throw debris.

3. Caught-in or between

These incidents happen when a worker is squeezed, crushed, or compressed: in a trench collapse, between equipment and a wall, or by being pulled into unguarded machinery.

How to prevent caught-in or between injuries

 Protect trenches 5 feet deep or more with sloping, shoring, or trench boxes (unless the excavation is in stable rock), and have a competent person inspect them daily.

 Keep spoils and equipment at least 2 feet back from trench edges.

 Keep guards on rotating parts and lock out equipment before servicing it.

 Never position yourself between moving equipment and an immovable object.

Remember: a cubic yard of soil can weigh as much as a small car. Trench collapses happen fast and leave almost no chance of escape.

4. Electrocution

Electrocutions come from contact with overhead power lines, energized parts, damaged tools and cords, and improperly grounded equipment.

How to prevent electrocution

 Locate overhead and underground lines before work starts, and keep equipment a safe distance away (generally at least 10 feet for lines up to 50 kV, more for higher voltages, and 20 feet for most crane work).

 Use ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) or an assured equipment grounding program.

 Inspect cords and tools; take damaged ones out of service.

 Lock out and tag out circuits before working on them.

 Never use metal ladders near electrical work.

Bringing the Focus Four onto your site

The best training ties these hazards to your actual work. In my on-site classes, we walk through where the Focus Four show up on your crew's projects, whether that's a roof edge, a trench on a utility job, or a lift near power lines, so the lessons stick when people get back to work. Book a Construction OSHA 10 or 30 for your team.

What is the difference between the Fatal Four and the Focus Four?
They're the same four hazards: falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution. OSHA now generally uses "Focus Four" to emphasize prevention.
What is the leading cause of death in construction?
Falls. They consistently cause more construction worker deaths than any other hazard, which is why fall protection is also OSHA's most frequently cited standard.
Is the Focus Four covered in OSHA 10 General Industry?
The Focus Four is a construction-specific module. General Industry courses cover related topics like walking-working surfaces, electrical safety, and machine guarding.
At what height is fall protection required in construction?
In construction, OSHA generally requires fall protection at 6 feet or more above a lower level. Scaffolds use a 10-foot threshold. See our fall protection guide for details.


---

# OSHA Fall Protection Requirements: Heights, Systems & Training

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/osha-fall-protection-requirements.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

OSHA requires fall protection at 4 feet in general industry, 6 feet in construction, 10 feet on scaffolds, and 5 feet in shipyards and 8 feet in longshoring. Protection can be guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall arrest systems, and employers must train workers to recognize fall hazards and use the equipment correctly.
Fall protection heights by industry

 SettingProtection required atStandard

 General industry (warehouses, plants, facilities)4 feet29 CFR 1910.28

 Shipyards5 feet29 CFR 1915

 Construction6 feet29 CFR 1926.501

 Longshoring8 feet29 CFR 1918

 Scaffolds (construction)10 feet29 CFR 1926.451

Regardless of height, OSHA requires protection when working over dangerous equipment or machinery, because a short fall onto a hazard can be just as deadly.

Acceptable fall protection systems

Guardrail systems

Guardrails are usually the best option because they protect everyone without depending on each worker to clip in. Key specs in construction:

 Top rail at 42 inches, plus or minus 3 inches, above the walking surface.

 Midrails, screens, or mesh between the top rail and the surface (midrails roughly halfway, at about 21 inches).

 Top rail must withstand 200 pounds of force applied outward or downward.

 Toe boards where tools or materials could fall on people below.

Personal fall arrest systems (PFAS)

A PFAS is an anchorage, a connector (lanyard or self-retracting lifeline), and a full-body harness. Requirements include:

 Anchorages that support 5,000 pounds per worker, or are designed and used under a qualified person's supervision with a safety factor of at least two.

 Rigged so a worker can't free fall more than 6 feet or contact any lower level.

 Body belts are not allowed for fall arrest. Use a full-body harness.

 Inspect the system before each use and remove any component that has arrested a fall.

 Have a rescue plan. A worker hanging in a harness needs to be reached quickly.

Safety nets

Nets must be installed as close as practical under the work surface, and never more than 30 feet below it, and they must be drop-tested or certified.

Other options

Depending on the work, OSHA also recognizes positioning devices, warning line systems and safety monitoring on low-slope roofs, controlled access zones, and covers for holes. Each has specific rules, and many only apply in limited situations.

Holes, skylights, and covers

Floor holes and skylights are some of the most overlooked fall hazards I see. Covers must:

 Support at least twice the weight of workers, equipment, and materials that may be on them.

 Be secured so they can't be displaced by wind, equipment, or workers.

 Be color-coded or marked "HOLE" or "COVER."

Ladders

Ladders are their own standard (and a top-cited one). The basics: extend portable ladders at least 3 feet above the landing, set them at the proper angle (about 1 foot out for every 4 feet up), keep three points of contact, never stand on the top step of a stepladder, and inspect ladders before use.

Training is a separate requirement

In construction, 29 CFR 1926.503 requires employers to train each worker who might be exposed to fall hazards, by a competent person, on:

 The nature of fall hazards in the work area.

 How to erect, maintain, inspect, and take down the fall protection systems used.

 How to use and operate guardrails, PFAS, nets, and other systems.

 The role of each worker in safety monitoring and fall protection plans.

The employer must keep a written certification of that training. "Fall protection - training requirements" is itself one of OSHA's ten most frequently cited standards.

From the field: When I teach fall protection on-site, we look at your actual anchor points, harnesses, and roof or deck conditions. That turns a generic lesson into something your crew can use the next morning.

Need fall protection training for your crew? Ask about a custom workshop alongside an OSHA 10 or 30 course.

What is OSHA's 6-foot rule?
In construction, 29 CFR 1926.501 generally requires fall protection whenever a worker is on a walking or working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 feet or more above a lower level.
What is the fall protection height for general industry?
4 feet. Under 29 CFR 1910.28, general industry employers must protect workers from falls of 4 feet or more to a lower level.
When is fall protection required on scaffolds?
In construction, workers on scaffolds more than 10 feet above a lower level must be protected by guardrails or personal fall arrest systems, depending on the scaffold type.
How high should a guardrail be?
The top rail must be 42 inches above the walking surface, plus or minus 3 inches, with a midrail roughly halfway between the top rail and the surface. It must withstand a 200-pound force applied outward or downward.
Does OSHA 10 count as fall protection training?
Not by itself. OSHA 10 covers fall hazards, but OSHA's fall protection training requirement calls for training on the specific hazards and systems used at your workplace, delivered by a competent person and documented.


---

# OSHA's Most Frequently Cited Standards and How to Avoid Them

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/most-cited-osha-standards.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

OSHA's most frequently cited standards consistently include fall protection (general requirements), hazard communication, ladders, respiratory protection, lockout/tagout, powered industrial trucks, fall protection training, scaffolding, eye and face protection, and machine guarding. Fall protection has been the number one citation for more than a decade.
The standards OSHA cites most

Here are the standards that consistently appear on OSHA's annual top 10, with the most common reasons employers get cited. Exact rankings shift slightly from year to year; check OSHA's current list for the latest order.

 StandardApplies toCommon problems

 Fall Protection: General Requirements (1926.501)ConstructionUnprotected edges, roofs, and holes at 6 feet or more

 Hazard Communication (1910.1200)All industriesNo written program, missing SDSs, unlabeled containers, no training

 Ladders (1926.1053)ConstructionLadders not extended 3 ft above landing, damaged ladders, using top step

 Respiratory Protection (1910.134)All industriesNo written program, no medical evaluations or fit tests

 Lockout/Tagout (1910.147)General industryNo energy control procedures, no periodic inspections, no training

 Powered Industrial Trucks (1910.178)General industryUntrained or unevaluated operators, damaged trucks left in service

 Fall Protection: Training (1926.503)ConstructionNo training by a competent person, no written certification

 Scaffolding (1926.451)ConstructionMissing guardrails, poor access, unsound footing, no competent person

 Eye and Face Protection (1926.102)ConstructionNo protection for flying particles, chemicals, or welding

 Machine Guarding (1910.212)General industryMissing or removed guards at points of operation

What the list tells you

Look closely and a pattern jumps out: a lot of these are paperwork and training problems. Hazard communication, respiratory protection, lockout/tagout, forklifts, and fall protection training all require written programs, documented training, or both. Employers often have the right equipment but can't show OSHA the program or records behind it.

A practical self-check

For construction sites

 Walk every edge, opening, and roof. Is anything 6 feet or higher unprotected?

 Check every ladder for damage, setup, and the 3-foot extension.

 Have a competent person inspect scaffolds before each shift.

 Confirm you have written certification of fall protection training for every exposed worker.

 Make sure eye and face protection is on hand and in use for cutting, grinding, nailing, and chemicals.

For facilities and general industry

 Is your hazard communication program written, and is every chemical container labeled with an SDS on file?

 Does every machine have written lockout/tagout procedures, and have you done your periodic inspection this year?

 Has every forklift operator been trained and evaluated, with an evaluation at least every three years?

 If anyone wears a respirator (other than voluntary dust mask use), do you have medical evaluations and annual fit tests on file?

 Walk the floor and look for missing or bypassed machine guards.

From the field: The supervisors who prevent citations are the ones who know what an inspector looks for. That's a big part of what OSHA 30 teaches, and why I recommend it for every foreman and facility lead.

What citations cost

OSHA penalties are adjusted for inflation every year and can exceed $16,000 per serious violation and $165,000 per willful or repeat violation. Read our guide to OSHA penalties and inspections for the details.

Want your supervisors to spot these problems before OSHA does? Book OSHA 30 for your leads.

What is OSHA's most cited standard?
Fall Protection - General Requirements (29 CFR 1926.501) in construction. It has been OSHA's most frequently cited standard every year for more than a decade.
Where does OSHA publish the top 10 list?
OSHA announces its preliminary top 10 most frequently cited standards each fiscal year and posts them on osha.gov. The list typically comes out in the fall.
Are these the most dangerous hazards?
Not exactly. The list shows what OSHA cites most often during inspections, which reflects both how common a hazard is and how often employers fall short. Several, like fall protection, are also major causes of deaths and serious injuries.
How can I check my site against this list?
Walk your site with the list in hand, review your written programs (HazCom, respiratory, lockout/tagout), and check training records. An OSHA 30 course is a good way to give supervisors the knowledge to do this regularly.


---

# OSHA Training in Illinois: A Guide for Chicagoland Employers and Workers

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/osha-training-requirements-illinois.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

In Illinois, federal OSHA covers private-sector employers, while Illinois OSHA (part of the Illinois Department of Labor) covers state and local government employees. State law doesn't broadly require OSHA 10 or 30 cards for private workers, but many Chicagoland contractors, project owners, unions, and public agencies require them. Authorized trainers like Zahid Presswala in Naperville offer on-site OSHA 10 and 30 classes across the region.
Who enforces OSHA in Illinois?

Illinois runs a public-sector-only state plan. That creates two systems:

 Employer typeCovered by

 Private companies: contractors, manufacturers, warehouses, retailers, healthcareFederal OSHA

 State agencies, counties, cities, villages, townships, school districts, public universitiesIllinois OSHA (Illinois Department of Labor)

Illinois OSHA's standards must be at least as effective as federal OSHA's, so the safety rules you'll learn in an OSHA 10 or 30 course apply on both sides.

Are OSHA 10 or 30 cards required in Illinois?

Unlike some states, Illinois doesn't have a broad law requiring every construction worker to hold an OSHA card. But that doesn't mean you can skip it. In the Chicago area, requirements usually come from:

 General contractors who require OSHA 10 for everyone on site and OSHA 30 for supervisors.

 Project owners such as hospitals, universities, airports, data centers, and large commercial developers.

 Public agencies and municipalities that write OSHA training into bid documents and contracts.

 Unions and apprenticeship programs that include Outreach training in their curriculum.

 Insurers and safety programs that reward documented training.

If you bid on larger projects in Cook, DuPage, Will, Kane, or Lake counties, plan on needing cards for your crew.

Tip for contractors: Don't wait until a project starts to discover your crew needs cards. A legitimate OSHA 10 takes at least two days and OSHA 30 at least four, so build training into your schedule before mobilization.

OSHA's employer training duties still apply

Even when no card is required, OSHA standards require employers to train workers on specific hazards they face, such as fall protection, hazard communication, forklifts, respirators, and lockout/tagout. An Outreach course is a strong foundation for that, but it doesn't replace site- and equipment-specific training.

Common industries we train in Chicagoland

 Construction: general contractors, framing and drywall, roofing, concrete, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and remodeling crews.

 Warehousing and logistics: distribution centers along I-55, I-80, and I-88 corridors.

 Manufacturing: plants and shops across DuPage, Kane, and Will counties.

 Facilities and property management: maintenance teams for commercial, residential, and institutional buildings.

Getting your crew trained in Illinois

I'm based in Naperville and teach OSHA 10 and 30 courses on-site throughout the region, including Chicago, Aurora, Joliet, Bolingbrook, Plainfield, Downers Grove, Oak Brook, Schaumburg, Elgin, and beyond. Classes are available in English, Gujarati, and Urdu, and every graduate receives an official DOL wallet card.

 Fill out the booking form with your industry, headcount, and dates.

 I'll confirm the course, location, and group pricing.

 We train at your site, and your crew gets carded.

Is OSHA 10 required in Illinois?
There's no broad Illinois law requiring every private-sector worker to hold an OSHA 10 card. In practice, many general contractors, project owners, public agencies, and unions in the Chicago area require OSHA 10 for workers and OSHA 30 for supervisors. Always check your contract and site rules.
Who enforces OSHA in Illinois?
Federal OSHA enforces workplace safety for private employers in Illinois through several area offices, including one in Aurora. Illinois OSHA, a division of the Illinois Department of Labor, covers state and local government workplaces.
Where can I take OSHA 10 near Naperville or Chicago?

Can OSHA training be held at our job site in Illinois?
Yes. On-site training is the most common format for crews. Zahid brings the course materials and teaches at your job site, shop, office, or a shared venue.

# Online vs In-Person OSHA Training: Which Is Better for Your Crew?

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/online-vs-in-person-osha-training.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

Both online and in-person OSHA Outreach courses earn the same DOL wallet card, as long as the provider is OSHA-authorized or OSHA-accepted. Online works well for one person who needs flexibility. In-person, on-site training usually works better for crews: it's interactive, tailored to your actual hazards, available in workers' preferred languages, and everyone finishes on the same schedule.
Online vs in-person at a glance

 OnlineIn-person / on-site

 CardDOL wallet card (from accepted providers)DOL wallet card (from authorized trainers)

 ScheduleSelf-paced, up to 6 months to finishFixed dates; group finishes together

 InteractionVideos, slides, quizzesLive discussion, Q&A, demonstrations

 Tailored to your siteNoYes

 LanguageUsually English or SpanishAny language the trainer speaks fluently

 Best forIndividuals needing flexibilityCrews, new hires, multilingual teams

When online training makes sense

 You're one person who needs a card and has a reliable computer and internet connection.

 Your schedule makes fixed class dates impossible.

 You're comfortable reading English or Spanish technical content on your own.

Just make sure the provider is on OSHA's list of accepted online Outreach providers. Plenty of sites sell "OSHA training" that doesn't lead to a DOL card.

When in-person training is the better choice

You're training a crew

With online courses, every worker progresses at a different pace. Some finish in a week, some take months, and some never finish. With an on-site class, the whole crew is done in two days (OSHA 10) or four (OSHA 30), and you know exactly when everyone will have their completion record.

You want training that fits your work

An online module can't look at your scaffold, your trench, or your loading dock. A live trainer can tie every topic back to the equipment and hazards your crew sees every day, and answer the "what about when we..." questions that always come up.

Your crew speaks more than one language

People learn safety best in the language they think in. Being able to explain a lockout procedure or a fall arrest system in Gujarati or Urdu, and not just English, makes a real difference for many crews I train.

Retention matters to you

Clicking "next" through slides isn't the same as discussing a near-miss with your coworkers. In my experience, crews that train together also hold each other accountable afterward.

A hybrid approach

Some employers do both: online OSHA 10 for a new hire who starts between classes, and on-site OSHA 10 or 30 for the main crew and supervisors. Either way, follow up with toolbox talks and task-specific training.

Ready to train your crew in person? Book an on-site class anywhere in Chicagoland.

Is an online OSHA 10 card legitimate?
Yes, if the course comes from an OSHA-accepted online Outreach provider. The card is the same DOL card you'd receive from an in-person class. Be cautious of sites that aren't on OSHA's accepted provider list.
Is in-person OSHA training more expensive?
Per person, it can be similar or less for groups. On-site training is usually priced for the whole group, and it saves the time workers spend struggling with modules alone. Request a quote to compare.
Can I do OSHA 10 online in one day?
No. Online Outreach courses also limit training to 7.5 hours per day, so OSHA 10 takes at least two days online too.
Can on-site training be taught in another language?
Yes. Outreach trainers can teach in any language they're fluent in. Zahid teaches in English, Gujarati, and Urdu.

# How to Verify an OSHA Card and Spot a Fake

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/how-to-verify-osha-card.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

There's no public national database of OSHA card holders. To verify an OSHA 10 or 30 card, check that it's an official Department of Labor card with the student's name, course, industry, and the issuing trainer or provider, then contact that trainer or provider to confirm the student completed the course. You can confirm the trainer is authorized in OSHA's Outreach trainer directory.
What a legitimate card looks like

OSHA 10 and 30 cards are issued through the U.S. Department of Labor's OSHA Outreach Training Program. A real card shows:

 The Department of Labor / OSHA Outreach Training Program identity.

 The course length (10-hour or 30-hour) and industry (Construction or General Industry).

 The student's name.

 Information identifying the authorized trainer or OSHA-accepted online provider.

Cards issued in recent years also include security features designed to make counterfeiting harder, and many providers offer a QR code or other verification method.

How to verify a card, step by step

 Look at the card itself. Check that it's a durable wallet card (not just a printed certificate), and that the name matches the worker's ID.

 Identify the trainer or provider. Note the trainer or online provider shown on or with the card.

 Confirm the trainer is authorized. Search OSHA's trainer directory for in-person trainers, or check OSHA's list of accepted online providers.

 Contact the trainer or provider. Ask them to confirm the student's name, course, and completion date. Use any QR code or verification tool they provide.

 Keep a copy. Store a photo or scan of the card with the worker's training records.

Red flags

Be suspicious if: the card was "earned" in a single day, the worker can't remember the trainer or any details of the class, the card has misspellings or poor printing, the provider only takes cash and gives no receipt, or the name doesn't match the worker's ID.

Federal investigators have charged people for selling fake OSHA cards, and contractors have been caught with workers on site who never took the training. Beyond the legal risk, a fake card means a worker who may not recognize the hazards that kill people in construction.

Temporary certificates vs official cards

When students finish a course, they often get a printable certificate or completion letter right away. That's a legitimate temporary record. The official card follows, and OSHA requires trainers to issue it within 90 days. If a worker only has a certificate from more than a few months ago, ask why.

Make verification easy

The simplest way to be sure your crew's cards are real is to train them yourself with an authorized trainer. When Zahid trains your crew on-site, you get a roster of everyone who completed the course, and every card comes from a verifiable OSHA-authorized trainer. Book a class.

Is there an online OSHA card lookup?
Not a public national one. OSHA doesn't publish a searchable list of card holders. Verification goes through the authorized trainer or online provider who issued the card. Some newer cards include a QR code or verification method from the provider.
What should a real OSHA 10 card show?
A legitimate card shows that it's from the U.S. Department of Labor OSHA Outreach Training Program, the course (10 or 30-hour), the industry (Construction or General Industry), the student's name, and information identifying the trainer or provider.
What happens if a worker has a fake card?
Using a fraudulent card can get a worker removed from a site, and knowingly selling fake cards has led to federal criminal charges. Employers who rely on fake cards may also fall short of contract or legal requirements.
How can I verify a trainer?
Search OSHA's authorized Outreach trainer directory by name. For example, Zahid Presswala's listing is publicly available on OSHA.gov.
