# OSHA Penalties and Inspections: What Employers Need to Know

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/osha-penalties-employers.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-25

OSHA penalties are adjusted for inflation each January. Maximums currently exceed $16,000 per serious or other-than-serious violation and $165,000 per willful or repeated violation, with daily penalties for failing to fix a cited hazard. Inspections are triggered by imminent danger, fatalities and severe injuries, complaints, referrals, and targeted programs. Documented training and written safety programs are among the best defenses.
Types of OSHA violations

 Violation typeWhat it meansMaximum penalty

 Other-than-seriousRelated to safety and health but unlikely to cause death or serious harmOver $16,000 per violation

 SeriousSubstantial probability of death or serious physical harm, and the employer knew or should have knownOver $16,000 per violation

 Failure to abateA cited hazard wasn't corrected by the deadlineOver $16,000 per day beyond the abatement date

 WillfulIntentional disregard of, or plain indifference to, the lawOver $165,000 per violation

 RepeatedSame or similar violation cited within the past five yearsOver $165,000 per violation

Amounts are adjusted for inflation each year. See OSHA's penalties page for exact current figures. Willful violations that cause a worker's death can also lead to criminal prosecution.

What triggers an inspection

OSHA can't inspect every workplace, so it prioritizes:

 Imminent danger situations.

 Fatalities and severe injuries reported by employers.

 Worker complaints about hazards or violations.

 Referrals from other agencies, organizations, or the media.

 Targeted inspections of high-hazard industries, including emphasis programs for falls, trenching, and other hazards.

 Follow-up inspections to confirm hazards were corrected.

In construction, inspectors often stop when they can see a hazard from the street, like workers on a roof with no fall protection or an unshored trench.

Reporting requirements

 Within 8 hours: any work-related fatality.

 Within 24 hours: any work-related inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye.

What happens during an inspection

 Opening conference: the compliance officer explains why they're there and the scope of the inspection.

 Walkaround: they tour the site, observe conditions, take photos and measurements, and may interview workers privately.

 Records review: expect requests for injury and illness logs, written programs (hazard communication, lockout/tagout, respiratory protection), and training records.

 Closing conference: they discuss apparent violations and possible ways to correct them.

Citations, if any, usually arrive later. Employers have 15 working days to contest them, and can request an informal conference to discuss settlement.

How to reduce your risk

 Train supervisors to see what inspectors see. An OSHA 30 course gives foremen and facility leads the knowledge to catch hazards on their daily walks.

 Give every worker OSHA 10. Workers who recognize hazards speak up before someone gets hurt.

 Keep your paperwork current. Many top citations, such as hazard communication, are about missing written programs and training records.

 Fix the big four first. Falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrical hazards. See our Focus Four guide.

 Use the top 10 list as a checklist. See OSHA's most cited standards.

Training is cheaper than a citation. Get a quote for on-site OSHA 10 or 30.

How much is an OSHA fine?
Maximum penalties are adjusted annually. They currently exceed $16,000 per serious or other-than-serious violation and $165,000 per willful or repeated violation. Check OSHA's penalties page for the current figures.
What triggers an OSHA inspection?
OSHA prioritizes imminent danger situations, then fatalities and severe injuries, worker complaints, referrals from other agencies or media, targeted inspections of high-hazard industries, and follow-up inspections.
When do I have to report an injury to OSHA?
Within 8 hours of a work-related fatality, and within 24 hours of an inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye.
Can OSHA penalties be reduced?
Yes. OSHA can reduce penalties based on employer size, good faith, and history. Employers can also request an informal conference or contest citations within 15 working days of receiving them.
Does OSHA training reduce penalties?
Training itself doesn't guarantee lower penalties, but documented training and effective safety programs help prevent violations, can support good-faith reductions, and are required by many standards.


---

# How Much Does OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 Training Cost?

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/osha-10-cost.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

As a general guide, online OSHA 10 courses from OSHA-authorized providers commonly cost about $60 to $90 per person, and online OSHA 30 courses about $160 to $200. In-person classes usually cost more per person, but on-site group training brings the per-worker price down as headcount grows. Prices well below these ranges, or promises of a card in one day, are warning signs of a fake card.
Typical OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 prices

There's no official price. OSHA authorizes trainers and online providers, and each sets its own rates. Here's what we commonly see in the market:

 FormatOSHA 10OSHA 30Notes

 Online (OSHA-authorized provider)About $60 to $90About $160 to $200Self-paced; limited to 7.5 hours per day

 In-person public classVaries, usually more than onlineVaries, usually more than onlineLive trainer, fixed dates and location

 On-site group classQuoted per groupQuoted per groupCost per worker drops as headcount rises

These are general ranges, not quotes. Prices change, and many providers run discounts or volume pricing.

What affects the price

 Course length. OSHA 30 is three times as long as OSHA 10 and costs more.

 Format. Online is cheapest per person; live training costs more but includes a real trainer.

 Group size. On-site classes spread the trainer's cost across everyone in the room.

 Location and travel. Training far from the trainer's base may include travel.

 Language. Finding an authorized trainer who teaches in your crew's language can be harder, but it pays off in understanding.

The real cost for employers

For a company, the sticker price is only part of the cost. Consider:

 Paid time and lost production while workers train, which is the same whichever format you choose.

 Travel time if you send people to an off-site class.

 Tracking who finished an online course, and who didn't.

 Effectiveness. Training that sticks prevents injuries and OSHA penalties, which can exceed $16,000 per serious violation.

That's why many contractors and facilities choose on-site group training: one class, everyone done, no travel.

Don't pay for a fake card

If an offer sounds too cheap or too fast, it probably is. Warning signs:

 An OSHA 10 finished in a single day, or OSHA 30 in under four days

 No way to verify the trainer on OSHA's website

 A "certificate" or plastic card that isn't the official DOL Outreach card

Read how to verify an OSHA card before you pay. You can verify Zahid on OSHA.gov.

Is OSHA 10 free anywhere?
Sometimes. Some unions, apprenticeship programs, workforce agencies, and employers pay for OSHA 10 for their members or workers. OSHA itself doesn't sell the course; authorized trainers and online providers do.
Who pays for OSHA training, the worker or the employer?
It depends. When OSHA 10 or 30 is a condition of a job or project, employers usually pay. Workers sometimes pay on their own to qualify for jobs. Separately, when OSHA standards require hazard-specific training, the employer must provide it at no cost to workers.
Why does in-person training cost more than online?
You're paying for a live, authorized trainer's time, travel, and the ability to tailor the course to your work. For groups, that cost is shared, so the price per worker often ends up competitive with online courses.
How much does on-site OSHA training cost for a group?
On-site classes are quoted based on the course, headcount, location, and schedule. Send those details through the booking form for a quote from Zahid.

# What Is Covered in OSHA 10? Topics for Construction and General Industry

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/what-is-covered-in-osha-10.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

OSHA 10-Hour Construction covers Introduction to OSHA (2 hours), the Focus Four hazards (falls, electrocution, struck-by, caught-in or between), personal protective equipment, and health hazards, plus electives such as scaffolds, ladders, and excavations. OSHA 10-Hour General Industry covers Introduction to OSHA, walking-working surfaces, exit routes and emergency action plans, electrical safety, PPE, and hazard communication, plus electives such as forklifts, machine guarding, and lockout/tagout.
OSHA 10-Hour Construction topics

OSHA 10 Construction follows the construction standards in 29 CFR 1926. The course outline includes:

 SectionTopics

 RequiredIntroduction to OSHA (2 hours): worker rights, employer responsibilities, filing a complaint, inspections

 RequiredOSHA Focus Four hazards (4 hours): falls, electrocution, struck-by, caught-in or between

 RequiredPersonal protective and lifesaving equipment

 RequiredHealth hazards in construction: noise, silica, lead, chemicals, heat

 ElectivesChosen by the trainer, such as cranes and rigging, excavations, materials handling, scaffolds, stairways and ladders, tools, or fire protection

 OptionalAny construction topic that fits the class, or more time on required topics

Read more about the Focus Four hazards, the heart of the construction course. Ready to train? See OSHA 10 Construction with Zahid.

OSHA 10-Hour General Industry topics

OSHA 10 General Industry follows 29 CFR 1910. The course outline includes:

 SectionTopics

 RequiredIntroduction to OSHA (2 hours)

 RequiredWalking and working surfaces, including fall protection

 RequiredExit routes, emergency action plans, fire prevention plans, and fire protection

 RequiredElectrical safety

 RequiredPersonal protective equipment

 RequiredHazard communication

 ElectivesSuch as hazardous materials, materials handling, machine guarding, lockout/tagout, powered industrial trucks, ergonomics, bloodborne pathogens, or safety and health programs

See OSHA 10 General Industry with Zahid.

How OSHA 30 compares

OSHA 30 covers everything above in more depth and adds a much longer list of topics, along with safety management for supervisors. Read OSHA 10 vs OSHA 30 to choose.

What OSHA 10 doesn't cover

OSHA 10 is an awareness course. It does not qualify anyone to operate a forklift, erect a scaffold, enter a confined space, or serve as a "competent person." Employers must still provide the task- and site-specific training OSHA standards require.

Is there a test at the end of OSHA 10?
OSHA requires trainers to confirm students learned the material. Online courses use quizzes and a final exam; in-person trainers use knowledge checks and participation.
Does OSHA 10 certify me to operate a forklift or scaffold?
No. OSHA 10 teaches hazard recognition. Tasks like forklift operation, scaffold erection, or respirator use require separate, specific training from your employer.
Can the trainer change the topics?
Trainers must teach OSHA's required topics but choose electives and examples. A good trainer tailors those to the crew's actual work.


---

# How Long Does OSHA 10 Take? OSHA 10 and 30 Timelines Explained

URL: https://oshawithzahid.com/guides/how-long-does-osha-10-take.html
Author: Zahid Presswala, OSHA Authorized Outreach Trainer
Updated: 2026-10-27

OSHA 10 takes at least two days and OSHA 30 takes at least four days, because OSHA limits Outreach training to a maximum of 7.5 hours per day, whether online or in person. Online courses must be finished within six months of starting. After you finish, authorized trainers must issue the official DOL wallet card within 90 days.
The 7.5-hour daily limit

OSHA's Outreach Training Program rules cap training at 7.5 hours per day. That's the reason the "10" and "30" can't be squeezed into one long day. The limit applies to in-person classes and online courses alike.

 CourseContact hoursMinimum daysCommon schedule

 OSHA 10 (Construction or General Industry)102Two consecutive days

 OSHA 30 (Construction or General Industry)304Four to five days, or one day a week for a month

How long each format takes

In-person and on-site classes

A live class follows a set schedule, so you know exactly when you'll be done: two days for OSHA 10, four or more for OSHA 30. On-site classes can be split into shorter sessions to fit shifts. See on-site OSHA training.

Online courses

Online courses are self-paced but still limited to 7.5 hours a day, and they must be completed within six months. In practice, many workers take a week or more to fit an online OSHA 10 around work.

When you get your card

 End of class: you receive proof of completion.

 Within 90 days: OSHA requires the trainer or provider to issue the official DOL wallet card.

If a job start date depends on your card, plan at least a couple of weeks ahead. Read how to get your OSHA 10 card for the full process.

Watch out for "fast" cards

Any offer to finish OSHA 10 in one day or OSHA 30 in two is a red flag. Learn how to verify an OSHA card.

Can you do OSHA 10 in one day?
No. OSHA's 7.5-hour daily limit means a legitimate OSHA 10 takes at least two days. A provider offering a one-day OSHA 10 is not following OSHA rules, and the card may not be valid.
How many days is OSHA 30?
At least four days. Many classes take four or five days, or are spread over several weeks.
How long do I have to finish an online OSHA course?
OSHA requires online Outreach courses to be completed within six months of the start date.
How long until I get my OSHA card?
You get proof of completion when you finish. OSHA requires the official wallet card to be issued within 90 days of course completion, and it often arrives sooner.
